source.version: arXiv:2406.07016v5 [cs.CL], 3 Jul 2025 (arXiv stamp, p. 1); document dated July 4, 2025. The search record carries the earlier title 'Delving into ChatGPT Usage in Academic Writing through Excess Vocabulary'; this version is retitled.
source.title_on_document: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary

paper_design_summary: The authors count, for each word and year, the share of 15.1 million English-language PubMed abstracts from 2010 to 2024 that contain the word. They compare observed 2024 frequencies with a counterfactual linear extrapolation from 2021 and 2022, find 'excess' style words, and use the frequency gap of sets of these marker words as a lower bound on the share of 2024 abstracts processed with LLMs. No people take part, nothing is randomized, and no creativity, novelty, or diversity outcome is measured.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. Corpus of published abstracts compared across years (2024 observed versus counterfactual extrapolated from 2021-2022).
assignment.quote: we study vocabulary changes in over 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010–2024 indexed by PubMed

participants.exclusions: Corpus filters: complete English-language abstracts of 250-4000 characters (24,814,136), restricted to publication years 2010-2024 (15,103,888); contaminating strings removed from 286,744 abstracts; 3,514 errata/correction/retraction notices erased (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.2).
participants.who: No human participants. Unit of analysis is the published abstract (and word-year frequencies).
participants.quote: We then only analyzed papers with publication years from 2010 to 2024, giving us 15 103 888 abstracts for analysis.

ai_tool.name_model: LLMs such as ChatGPT (not observed directly; inferred from vocabulary)
ai_tool.how_used: Not observed. The paper infers LLM processing of abstracts at the corpus level from excess style-word frequencies.

task.description: Scientific abstract writing (biomedical publications indexed by PubMed); not a creative or ideation task.

outcomes.name: Frequency gap of excess style marker words (lower bound on share of 2024 abstracts processed with LLMs)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Delta_G = P_G - Q_G, the observed minus counterfactual expected fraction of 2024 abstracts containing at least one word from a marker set G; counterfactual q = p_-2 + 2*max{p_-2 - p_-3, 0}. Two sets: 291 rare excess style words (frequency below T = 0.02) and 10 common words. Measures how much LLM text exists, not diversity or creativity.

contrasts.reported: Delta_rare = 0.136 (291 words); Delta_common = 0.134 (10 words); Delta = (Delta_common + Delta_rare)/2 = 0.135 (13.5%). Covid comparison: covid, pandemic, coronavirus, sars in 2021, Delta = 0.069. Subgroups: computation/bioinformatics ~0.20; UK and Australia ~0.05; China, South Korea, Taiwan ~0.20; Sensors 0.25; Cureus 0.20; MDPI 0.21; Frontiers 0.20; Nature+Science+Cell 0.07; Nature family 0.10; Korea x Sensors 0.34; China x computation 0.41. No standard errors or intervals.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.2 and Figure 5a; p. 4-5, Section 2.3 and Figure 5b-e

company_involvement.description: Funding listed: Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (KO6282/2-1), Gemeinnützige Hertie-Stiftung, IMPRS-IS, Excellence cluster 2064, NSF CAREER IIS-1943506. No AI company involvement stated.

data_and_code.data_url: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/download (raw PubMed); yearly word-occurrence matrix and annotations in https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab

eligibility.reason: Corpus study of PubMed abstracts with no human participants and no random assignment. Its outcome is excess word frequency used to bound how much LLM-processed text exists, with no diversity, similarity, novelty, or originality outcome, so it does not qualify as observational context either (codebook section 3: 'studies that measure how much AI text exists with no diversity outcome' are listed in the screening report and omitted). Homogenisation is mentioned only in the Discussion, citing other work (p. 6).

one_line_finding: Excess style-word frequencies in 15.1 million PubMed abstracts imply that at least 13.5 percent of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs (Delta = 0.135, average of 0.136 rare-word and 0.134 common-word gaps), about twice the 2021 Covid-vocabulary gap of 0.069 (p. 4, Section 2.2, Figure 5a).
notes: No people, no randomization, no creativity or diversity measure. The single outcome is recorded with question 'none' for documentation only. Number of excess words: 454 in 2024 versus up to 190 in 2021 (343 vs 180 unique lemmas); 379 excess style words in 2024 (p. 3, Figures 3 and S5). Unit of the frequency analysis is the abstract, aggregated per word and year; n_units gives abstracts analyzed.
